title: Photosynthesis, Respiration and Growth
bigQuestion: How does the energy in sunlight end up moving your muscles, and how does one cell become a body?

story.title: The Mouse, the Mint and the Air That Came Back
story.kicker: A candle goes out in a sealed jar. A week later, with nothing added but a sprig of mint, it burns again.
paragraphs: In 1771, in the English town of Leeds, a minister named Joseph Priestley was playing with jars. He lived next to a brewery, and the heavy gas that pooled over the fermenting vats fascinated him. He learned that a candle under a sealed glass jar burns for a while and then goes out. The air inside had been spoiled somehow. A mouse placed in that spoiled air could not live in it. Nothing anyone did, shaking it, cooling it, waiting, seemed to make the air good again.

Then Priestley tried a plant. He set a sprig of mint in a glass of water and slid the whole thing under a jar in which a candle had already burned out. He expected the plant to die. Instead it kept growing. After about ten days he lowered a lit candle into the jar and it burned as brightly as in fresh air. He tried a mouse. The mouse was fine. Something about the living plant had repaired the air that a flame had ruined.

Priestley repeated the test again and again through 1772, with mint, with spinach, with other greens. He reported to the Royal Society that plants restore air injured by burning or breathing, and the Society gave him its highest medal. What he could not explain was why. He did not know that the candle had used up the air's oxygen and filled the jar with carbon dioxide, or that the mint had quietly taken in that carbon dioxide and given back oxygen. Those words did not yet exist.

Others soon added pieces. In 1779 a Dutch doctor, Jan Ingenhousz, showed the trick only worked in sunlight and only with the green parts of a plant; in the dark, plants spoiled the air just as a mouse did. A few years later, chemists found that the plant was taking in a gas and building it into its own body. It took two more centuries, and radioactive carbon and electron microscopes, to trace every step of what happens inside the mint leaf.

Priestley's jar holds this whole chapter. On one side is a plant, catching light and building sugar out of thin air. On the other is a mouse, and a candle, and you, taking that sugar and that oxygen apart to release the energy. Between them is a loop that has run on Earth for billions of years, and it ends in the last question of the chapter: how a single cell uses that energy to divide, specialize, and become a mouse.
story.think: Priestley found that mint restored spoiled air but did not know why. What experiment would you design to figure out whether the plant was adding something to the jar or removing something from it?

lessons.title: Where a Tree's Weight Comes From
lessons.mainIdea: Plants build almost all their mass from carbon dioxide taken from the air, not from soil.
reading: Ask people where a tree's weight comes from and most say the soil. It seems obvious. Roots are in the dirt, and the tree grows. Around 1640 a Flemish physician, Jan Baptist van Helmont, tested the idea. He weighed a young willow at 5 pounds and planted it in a tub with 200 pounds of dried soil. He added only water for five years, covering the tub so no dust could fall in. Then he weighed everything again. The willow had grown to 169 pounds. The soil had lost about 2 ounces.

The soil was not the answer. Van Helmont concluded the tree was made of water, which was closer than soil but still wrong. The real source was invisible to him: the air. A tree is mostly carbon, and that carbon enters as *carbon dioxide* gas through tiny pores in the leaves called *stomata*. Water from the roots supplies the hydrogen. A tree's wood is, quite literally, air and water, rearranged and held together with energy from sunlight.

This is *photosynthesis*, from Greek words meaning putting together with light. In a green leaf, the pigment *chlorophyll* absorbs red and blue light and reflects green, which is why leaves look green to us. That absorbed light energy is used to pull carbon dioxide and water apart and reassemble them into sugar, mainly *glucose*, with oxygen gas as the leftover. The overall recipe fits on one line: six carbon dioxides plus six waters, with light, make one glucose and six oxygens.

Every bite of food you have ever eaten traces back to this reaction, either directly, from a plant, or through an animal that ate one. The oxygen you are breathing came from it too. When you next see a cornfield outside Chicago, remember that those stalks, tons of them per acre by September, were built almost entirely out of the carbon dioxide in the air above the field.

words.d: the process in which plants use light energy to build sugar from carbon dioxide and water
a gas in the air, made of one carbon and two oxygen atoms, that plants take in
the green pigment in plants that absorbs light energy
tiny pores in a leaf that let gases in and out
the simple sugar that photosynthesis produces and cells burn for energy

look.title: The Willow in the Tub
look.text: Van Helmont wrote that he planted a willow weighing five pounds in an earthen pot holding two hundred pounds of dried soil, watered it with rainwater or distilled water for five years, and kept the pot covered against dust. At the end the tree weighed 169 pounds and about three ounces, while the soil, dried again, had lost only about two ounces. He concluded that the tree's added weight had come from water alone.
look.cite: Jan Baptist van Helmont, Ortus Medicinae, published 1648
look.prompt: Van Helmont's measurements were careful and his conclusion was wrong. What ingredient could he not have weighed, and how would you show it mattered?

check.q: After five years, van Helmont's willow gained about 164 pounds while the soil lost about 2 ounces. What does this rule out?
choices: That the tree's mass came mainly from the soil
That the tree needed water
That the tree needed sunlight
That the tree was alive
check.why: If the tree had been built from soil, the soil would have lost about as much as the tree gained. It barely changed.

check.q: Where does most of the carbon in a tree's wood come from?
choices: Minerals dissolved in groundwater
Carbon dioxide gas in the air
The seed it grew from
Dead leaves in the soil
check.why: Carbon enters the plant as carbon dioxide through the stomata and is built into sugar and then into wood.

check.q: Why do most leaves look green?
choices: Green light is the most useful for photosynthesis
Chlorophyll produces green light
Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light and reflects green
Leaves contain green carbon dioxide
check.why: The light we see coming from a leaf is the light it did not absorb. Chlorophyll takes red and blue and sends green back.

lessons.title: Inside the Chloroplast
lessons.mainIdea: Photosynthesis happens in two stages: light energy is captured first, then that energy is used to build sugar from carbon dioxide.
reading: A leaf cell may hold dozens of *chloroplasts*, each a green oval about the size of a bacterium. Inside each one, stacks of flat membrane discs sit in a thick fluid. The discs are the *thylakoids*, and their membranes are packed with chlorophyll. The fluid around them is the *stroma*. The two locations do two different jobs, and photosynthesis is really two linked processes that happen a few nanometers apart.

The first stage runs in the thylakoid membranes and needs light, so it is called the light-dependent stage. When a chlorophyll molecule absorbs a photon, an electron in it jumps to a higher energy level. That energized electron is passed along a chain of proteins in the membrane, and the energy it gives up is used to make two energy-carrying molecules, ATP and a related molecule called NADPH. To replace the lost electrons, the chloroplast splits water molecules. The hydrogen is kept; the oxygen is released as gas. The oxygen a plant gives off comes from water, not from carbon dioxide, a fact proved in 1941 by tracking a heavy form of oxygen through the reaction.

The second stage runs in the stroma and does not need light directly, only the ATP and NADPH from stage one. Here an enzyme grabs carbon dioxide from the air and attaches it to a five-carbon sugar. A cycle of reactions, worked out in the 1950s by Melvin Calvin using radioactive carbon as a tracer, rearranges the carbons and spends the ATP and NADPH to build a three-carbon sugar. Two of those make a glucose. The plant then links glucoses into starch to store, into cellulose to build, or ships them as sucrose to roots and fruits.

Notice what the plant has done. It turned light, which cannot be stored, into chemical bonds, which can. A potato in a cellar in February holds sunlight from August. The energy in glucose is real: burn a gram of sugar and it releases about 4 kilocalories, the same energy your cells will get from it, only more slowly and in smaller, usable steps.

words.d: the organelle in plant cells where photosynthesis takes place
a flattened membrane disc inside a chloroplast where light is captured
the fluid inside a chloroplast where sugar is built from carbon dioxide
a single packet of light energy

look.title: The Two-Room Factory
look.text: Imagine a factory with two rooms. In the first room, sunlight is turned into charged batteries, and water is split to keep the line running, with oxygen vented out a chimney. In the second room, workers use those batteries to weld carbon dioxide from the air into sugar. At night the first room goes dark. The second room keeps going as long as charged batteries remain.
look.prompt: If a plant is kept in bright light but its stomata are sealed shut with wax so no carbon dioxide can enter, which room stops first? What builds up?

check.q: Where does the oxygen released by a plant come from?
choices: From glucose breaking apart
From carbon dioxide
From the soil
From water molecules that are split in the light-dependent stage
check.why: Water is split to replace the electrons chlorophyll loses. Its oxygen is the gas the plant releases, as tracer experiments showed.

check.q: What is the role of ATP and NADPH in photosynthesis?
choices: They carry energy from the light-capturing stage to the sugar-building stage
They are the pigments that absorb light
They are the sugars the plant stores
They are the gases the plant exchanges with the air
check.why: The light-dependent reactions charge these molecules; the Calvin cycle spends them to build sugar.

check.q: How did Melvin Calvin work out the steps by which carbon dioxide becomes sugar?
choices: By weighing plants before and after a day in the sun
By feeding algae radioactive carbon dioxide and tracking where the carbon went over seconds
By looking at chloroplasts with a light microscope
By burning leaves and measuring the ash
check.why: Radioactive carbon acted as a tracer. Stopping the reaction at different times showed which molecules held the carbon in what order.

lessons.title: What Slows a Plant Down
lessons.mainIdea: Photosynthesis runs only as fast as its scarcest input allows: light, carbon dioxide, water or the right temperature.
reading: A tomato plant on a windowsill in Rockford grows slowly in March and fast in June, even if it is watered the same. Sunlight is the difference. Photosynthesis, like any factory, runs at the pace of whatever it is shortest of. Biologists call the scarce ingredient the *limiting factor*. Add more of it and the rate climbs. Add more of something else and nothing changes. Finding the limiting factor is how greenhouse growers decide what to change.

Light is the first factor. In dim light, a plant makes sugar more slowly than it burns it and can starve in a bright room. As light increases, the rate rises, then levels off when something else runs short. Often that something is carbon dioxide, which is only about 0.04 percent of air. Commercial greenhouses sometimes pump extra carbon dioxide into the air around their tomatoes and cucumbers to lift the ceiling. Outdoors in a cornfield on a still July afternoon, the air right among the leaves can be measurably lower in carbon dioxide than the air above, because the plants are using it faster than the wind replaces it.

Temperature matters because the sugar-building stage is run by enzymes, and enzymes have a range they work in. Below about 10 degrees Celsius most crop plants slow to a crawl. Above roughly 40 degrees their enzymes begin to lose shape. Water matters in two ways. It is an ingredient, and it also controls the stomata. A thirsty plant closes its stomata to save water, which also shuts out carbon dioxide. On a hot, dry afternoon a plant may effectively stop photosynthesis to avoid drying out, even in full sun.

These limits explain a lot of the map of Illinois. Corn and soybeans are planted after the soil warms in spring and grow fastest in the long, warm, wet days of June and July. A dry August cuts the harvest even if the sky is clear, because closed stomata mean no carbon coming in. Farmers, growers and the scientists at the state's agricultural research stations watch light, water and temperature closely, because whichever one is scarcest sets the size of the crop.

words.d: the one input in shortest supply that sets the pace of a process
how much of something happens in a set amount of time
a glass or plastic building where growers control light, warmth, water and air for plants

look.title: The Greenhouse Puzzle
look.text: A grower runs three identical greenhouses of lettuce in January. House A gets extra lamps. House B gets extra carbon dioxide pumped in. House C gets both. After three weeks, A and B each grew a little more than a control house, but C grew much more than either.
look.prompt: Explain the result using the idea of a limiting factor. Why did fixing one shortage give a small gain, while fixing both gave a large one?

check.q: A plant in a sealed, well-lit terrarium stops growing. Which input is most likely limiting?
choices: Sunlight
Temperature
Carbon dioxide, which is used up and cannot be replaced in the sealed container
Chlorophyll
check.why: Light is plentiful, but the small amount of carbon dioxide in the sealed air is quickly consumed.

check.q: Why can a hot, dry afternoon nearly stop photosynthesis in full sun?
choices: Chlorophyll stops absorbing light when it is hot
The plant runs out of water to split
Heat destroys carbon dioxide
The plant closes its stomata to save water, which also blocks carbon dioxide from entering
check.why: Stomata cannot let water out without letting carbon dioxide in. Closing them to save water starves the leaf of carbon.

check.q: A greenhouse in winter already has strong lamps. Adding still more lamps does not increase growth, but adding carbon dioxide does. What does this show?
choices: Carbon dioxide was the limiting factor and light was not
Light was the limiting factor
The plants had too much water
The lamps were broken
check.why: Adding more of a non-limiting input changes nothing. Adding the limiting input raises the rate.

lessons.title: ATP, the Cell's Spending Money
lessons.mainIdea: Cells do not use glucose directly; they convert its energy into ATP, a small molecule that powers work in tiny, controlled payments.
reading: A gram of sugar holds about 4 kilocalories. If a cell released all of that at once it would cook itself. Instead, cells move energy in small, safe amounts using a molecule called *ATP*, adenosine triphosphate. Think of glucose as a hundred-dollar bill: valuable, but no vending machine takes it. ATP is the pocket change. A cell breaks the big bill into thousands of coins and spends them one at a time.

ATP is a small molecule with a tail of three phosphate groups. The bond holding the last phosphate on is under strain, because phosphates are negatively charged and repel one another. Snap that last phosphate off and energy is released, enough to power one step of work: one twitch of a muscle protein, one turn of a pump, one link added to a growing protein. What is left is *ADP*, adenosine diphosphate, with two phosphates. Add the phosphate back, using energy from food, and you have ATP again.

That recharge cycle runs constantly. A single ATP molecule in your body is used and rebuilt hundreds of times a day. Your cells hold only a few grams of ATP at any moment, yet over a full day they turn over roughly your own body mass in it. Nearly all that recharging happens in mitochondria, using the energy in glucose and oxygen. Stop the supply of oxygen, and the recharging stops within minutes. Brain cells, which cannot store much ATP, are the first to fail.

Every process from earlier chapters that needed energy needed ATP. Active transport pumps run on it. Ribosomes building proteins spend it. Cilia beat with it. Fireflies over a summer field in central Illinois make their light by using ATP to drive a reaction in a chemical called luciferin. The rest of this section asks the obvious question: how does a cell get the energy out of glucose and into ATP without setting itself on fire?

words.d: adenosine triphosphate, the molecule cells use to carry energy to where work is done
adenosine diphosphate, what remains when ATP gives up one phosphate; it is recharged back to ATP
a small charged group of one phosphorus and four oxygen atoms
a unit of energy; the calorie printed on food labels

look.title: Coins, Not Bills
look.text: A friend argues that ATP is silly. If the energy is already in glucose, why not just use glucose directly and skip the middle step? You reply with two facts: a burning sugar cube gives off its energy in one hot flash, and a muscle fiber needs to contract in thousands of tiny, separate pulls, each one paid for on the spot.
look.prompt: Why is a small, rechargeable energy carrier better for a cell than releasing glucose's energy all at once?

check.q: What happens when ATP releases energy?
choices: It gains a fourth phosphate
Its last phosphate is removed, leaving ADP
It breaks into two glucose molecules
It absorbs oxygen
check.why: Snapping off the strained third phosphate releases usable energy. The ADP left behind can be recharged.

check.q: Why do cells convert the energy in glucose into ATP instead of using glucose directly?
choices: Glucose contains no energy
ATP is larger and holds more energy
ATP releases energy in small, controlled amounts suited to single steps of work
Glucose cannot enter cells
check.why: Glucose holds a lot of energy at once. ATP delivers it in bite-sized payments to pumps, motors and enzymes.

check.q: If oxygen to the brain is cut off, why do brain cells fail within minutes?
choices: Oxygen is needed to build DNA
Brain cells are the largest cells and need the most oxygen
Brain cells use oxygen to make chlorophyll
ATP recharging in mitochondria depends on oxygen, and brain cells store very little ATP
check.why: Without oxygen the mitochondria cannot rebuild ATP fast enough, and brain cells have almost no reserve.

lessons.title: Cellular Respiration
lessons.mainIdea: Cellular respiration takes glucose apart in stages, using oxygen, and captures most of the released energy as ATP inside mitochondria.
reading: Photosynthesis run backward, roughly, is *cellular respiration*: one glucose plus six oxygens becomes six carbon dioxides plus six waters, and energy is released. It is the same overall change as burning sugar, but a cell does it in dozens of small enzyme-controlled steps, catching the energy a little at a time in ATP. The carbon dioxide you breathe out is the carbon that was in your last meal, and before that in a plant.

The first stage, *glycolysis*, happens in the cytoplasm and needs no oxygen. Enzymes split the six-carbon glucose into two three-carbon molecules called pyruvate. This yields only 2 ATP net, a small down payment. If oxygen is present, the pyruvate enters a *mitochondrion*. There, in a cycle of reactions worked out by Hans Krebs in 1937, the carbons are stripped off one by one as carbon dioxide, and their high-energy electrons are loaded onto carrier molecules.

The real payoff comes in the inner membrane of the mitochondrion, which is folded into deep creases to increase its surface area. Those electrons are passed down a chain of proteins, and at each step the energy released pumps hydrogen ions across the membrane, building up a gradient. The ions flow back through a turbine-like enzyme that spins and snaps phosphates onto ADP. At the end of the chain, oxygen accepts the spent electrons and joins with hydrogen to form water. That is why you need oxygen: it is the final electron catcher. Without it, the whole chain backs up and stops.

Count it up and one glucose yields roughly 30 ATP by the full aerobic route, about fifteen times what glycolysis alone provides. This is why a heart cell is crowded with mitochondria and why your breathing speeds up when you climb stairs. The idea that a hydrogen ion gradient drives ATP production was proposed by Peter Mitchell in 1961 and was doubted for years before experiments confirmed it. It turned out to be the same trick chloroplasts use in the thylakoid, one more sign that the two processes are deep relatives.

words.d: the process in which cells break down glucose using oxygen to make ATP, releasing carbon dioxide and water
the first stage of breaking down glucose, in the cytoplasm, which does not need oxygen
the organelle where the oxygen-using stages of respiration make most of a cell's ATP
using oxygen

look.title: ATP from One Glucose
look.cite: modern textbook estimate, rounded; older books give 36 to 38
look.prompt: About how many times more ATP does a cell get from glucose when oxygen is available? What does this predict about how much sugar an oxygen-starved cell must burn to do the same work?

check.q: What is the role of oxygen in cellular respiration?
choices: It accepts the used electrons at the end of the chain, forming water
It splits glucose in the cytoplasm
It is turned into carbon dioxide
It carries ATP out of the mitochondrion
check.why: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor. Without it, electrons have nowhere to go and the energy-capturing chain halts.

check.q: Where does glycolysis happen, and what does it need?
choices: In the mitochondrion, and it needs oxygen
In the cytoplasm, and it does not need oxygen
In the chloroplast, and it needs light
In the nucleus, and it needs DNA
check.why: Glycolysis is the ancient first step, run in the cytoplasm by enzymes, with no oxygen required.

check.q: The inner membrane of a mitochondrion is deeply folded. Why does that matter?
choices: The folds store glucose
The folds let oxygen enter more easily
The folds provide more surface area for the electron chain and the ATP-making enzymes
The folds keep the mitochondrion from bursting
check.why: More membrane means more room for the protein chains that pump ions and build ATP.

lessons.title: Energy Without Oxygen
lessons.mainIdea: When oxygen runs out, cells fall back on fermentation, which keeps glycolysis going but yields far less ATP.
reading: Bread rises. Muscles burn near the end of a sprint. Milk turns into yogurt. All three are the same emergency plan. When a cell cannot get enough oxygen, the electron chain in its mitochondria stalls, and the carrier molecules that glycolysis needs are stuck full of electrons. Glycolysis would stop too, and with it the last trickle of ATP. *Fermentation* is the workaround. The cell dumps the extra electrons onto pyruvate, freeing the carriers, so glycolysis can keep making its 2 ATP per glucose.

Yeast dumps the electrons by turning pyruvate into ethanol and carbon dioxide. This is *alcoholic fermentation*. Bakers want the carbon dioxide: the bubbles it makes in dough are what lift a loaf, and the ethanol bakes off in the oven. Brewers and winemakers want the ethanol. In 1857 Louis Pasteur showed that fermentation was the work of living yeast cells, not a simple chemical decay, and he found that yeast fermented most when kept away from air. Give it oxygen and it switches to respiration and grows instead.

Your muscle cells cannot make ethanol. They turn pyruvate into *lactic acid* instead. During hard exercise, your heart and lungs cannot deliver oxygen as fast as the muscles use ATP, so the cells switch partly to lactic acid fermentation. It is fast but wasteful, and lactic acid builds up until you slow down. Once you stop and gasp for a minute, oxygen catches up, the lactic acid is carried to the liver and rebuilt into glucose, and normal respiration resumes. That extra breathing after a race is you paying off the debt.

The same bacteria that sour milk into yogurt and cabbage into sauerkraut use lactic acid fermentation, and the acid they make is what keeps other microbes from spoiling the food. Fermentation is also a window into the past. Glycolysis and fermentation work with no oxygen, and Earth's early atmosphere had almost none. The first cells, billions of years ago, likely lived this way. The oxygen-using stages came later, after photosynthesis had filled the air with oxygen to catch the electrons.

words.d: a way of releasing energy from glucose without oxygen that yields only the ATP from glycolysis
fermentation by yeast that produces ethanol and carbon dioxide
the product of fermentation in muscle cells and in the bacteria that make yogurt
the three-carbon molecule that glycolysis makes from glucose

look.title: Pasteur Watches the Yeast
look.text: Pasteur reported that when he sowed a small amount of yeast in a sugar solution and kept it from contact with air, the yeast fermented the sugar vigorously while multiplying only a little. With air, the yeast multiplied far more but fermented far less sugar for each cell it made. He concluded that fermentation was life carried on without air.
look.cite: Louis Pasteur, memoir on alcoholic fermentation, Paris, late 1850s
look.prompt: Why would yeast grow faster with air but ferment more sugar without it? Use what you know about ATP yields.

check.q: What is the main purpose of fermentation for a cell?
choices: To make more ATP than respiration
To produce oxygen
To build glucose from carbon dioxide
To keep glycolysis running when oxygen is not available
check.why: Fermentation frees the electron carriers so glycolysis can continue making its small ATP yield without oxygen.

check.q: What makes bread dough rise?
choices: Carbon dioxide gas released by yeast fermentation
Oxygen released by yeast
Lactic acid expanding in the oven
Water evaporating from the dough
check.why: Yeast ferments sugars into ethanol and carbon dioxide; the gas bubbles are trapped in the dough.

check.q: Why do you keep breathing hard for a minute after a sprint?
choices: Your lungs are damaged by the effort
Your body needs extra oxygen to clear the lactic acid built up during fermentation and return to normal respiration
Your muscles are still fermenting
Your heart needs oxygen to make lactic acid
check.why: Hard exercise creates an oxygen debt. Extra breathing supplies the oxygen to process the lactic acid and rebuild ATP stores.

lessons.title: The Carbon Loop
lessons.mainIdea: Photosynthesis and respiration pass the same carbon atoms back and forth, and the whole planet breathes in a yearly rhythm.
reading: Put the two processes side by side. Photosynthesis takes in carbon dioxide and water, stores energy, and releases oxygen. Respiration takes in oxygen and sugar, releases energy, and gives back carbon dioxide and water. The outputs of each are the inputs of the other. A carbon atom in a corn kernel in Illinois was in the air over that field in July. Eaten by a hog, it becomes part of a cell, is burned for energy, and returns to the air as carbon dioxide, ready for a leaf to catch it again next summer.

Plants do both. A leaf runs respiration all the time, day and night, in its mitochondria, because it needs ATP just as you do. In daylight, photosynthesis usually runs faster than respiration, so the leaf takes in more carbon than it gives off, and the plant gains mass. At night it only respires, and Ingenhousz was right that a plant in the dark spoils the air a little. Over a year, a growing forest is a net absorber of carbon. A forest that is rotting or burning is a net source.

You can see the planet doing this. Since 1958 a station on Mauna Loa in Hawaii has measured carbon dioxide in clean mid-Pacific air. The record shows a sawtooth. Every spring and summer, as the vast forests and fields of the Northern Hemisphere leaf out and photosynthesize, the number drops by several parts per million. Every autumn and winter, as leaves fall and rot and photosynthesis slows, it rises again. The Northern Hemisphere has most of Earth's land, so its growing season sets the rhythm. Earth inhales in May and exhales in October.

Under the sawtooth, the yearly average has climbed steadily, from about 317 parts per million in 1960 to over 400 today. That rise is not from respiration. It comes mostly from burning coal, oil and gas, which releases carbon that photosynthesis buried underground hundreds of millions of years ago, faster than today's plants and oceans can take it back up. Fossil fuel is ancient sunlight. Burning it is respiration on a planetary scale, without the matching photosynthesis.

words.d: the movement of carbon atoms between air, living things, soil, oceans and rock
the amount left after subtracting what goes out from what comes in
a unit for a small share of a mixture; 400 ppm means 400 molecules out of every million
coal, oil or natural gas, formed from living things buried long ago

look.title: Carbon Dioxide in the Air at Mauna Loa
look.cite: NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory, Mauna Loa record, rounded
look.prompt: By about how much did the yearly average rise between 1960 and 2020? The seasonal up-and-down each year is only a few parts per million. What does that comparison tell you about the two causes?

check.q: How are photosynthesis and cellular respiration related?
choices: They are the same process in different organisms
Only plants do photosynthesis and only animals do respiration
The outputs of each are the inputs of the other, so carbon cycles between them
Respiration happens by day and photosynthesis by night
check.why: Photosynthesis stores energy in sugar and releases oxygen; respiration uses oxygen to release that energy and returns carbon dioxide.

check.q: Why does the carbon dioxide level at Mauna Loa fall every Northern Hemisphere summer?
choices: Summer heat destroys carbon dioxide
Ocean water absorbs more gas when warm
People burn less fuel in summer
Leafing-out plants across the Northern Hemisphere take up more carbon dioxide than they release
check.why: The Northern Hemisphere holds most of Earth's land plants. Their summer photosynthesis draws carbon dioxide down for a few months.

check.q: A plant is kept in complete darkness for two days. What gas exchange will it show?
choices: It will take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide, because only respiration is running
It will take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen
It will exchange no gases at all
It will release both oxygen and carbon dioxide
check.why: Without light there is no photosynthesis, but the plant's mitochondria keep respiring to make ATP.

lessons.title: The Cell Cycle
lessons.mainIdea: A cell grows, copies its DNA, checks its work, and only then divides, in a cycle that takes about a day for many human cells.
reading: You replace the entire lining of your gut about every week, and you replace your skin's outer layer about every month. Every second, your bone marrow releases millions of new red blood cells. All of that comes from cells dividing, and each division is the end of a repeating sequence called the *cell cycle*. A cell that divides on schedule keeps you alive. One that divides off schedule is the subject of a later lesson.

Most of the cycle is *interphase*, when the cell looks calm under a microscope but is working hard. In the first gap phase, G1, it grows, makes proteins and organelles, and decides whether conditions are right to continue. In the S phase, S for synthesis, it copies every one of its chromosomes so that there are two complete sets of DNA. In the second gap, G2, it grows more and checks the copies. Only then comes M phase, mitosis, when the two sets are pulled apart and the cell splits.

The cycle has *checkpoints*, moments when the cell pauses and takes stock. Is it big enough? Is there enough food? Is the DNA damaged? Was every chromosome copied exactly once? A protein called p53 is one of the inspectors; if it finds broken DNA it halts the cycle until repairs are made, or if the damage is too great, orders the cell to destroy itself. Checkpoints are why most damaged cells never become tumors. They are the quality control of the body.

Different cells run the cycle at different speeds. Human cells growing in a lab dish take about 24 hours to go around once. Cells lining the gut divide faster. Mature nerve and heart muscle cells mostly leave the cycle altogether and never divide again, which is why damage to the brain or heart heals so poorly. Liver cells sit quietly for years but can re-enter the cycle when the liver is injured, which is why a liver can regrow much of itself after surgery.

words.d: the repeating sequence of growth, DNA copying and division in a cell's life
the long part of the cell cycle between divisions, when the cell grows and copies its DNA
a point in the cell cycle where the cell pauses to confirm it is ready to continue
a single long DNA molecule with its proteins; human body cells have 46

look.title: A Day in the Life of a Dividing Human Cell
look.cite: typical textbook values for cells grown in the lab, rounded
look.prompt: What fraction of the cycle is spent actually dividing? If you looked at 100 of these cells at random, about how many would you expect to catch in mitosis?

check.q: During which phase does a cell copy all of its DNA?
choices: G1
S
G2
M
check.why: S stands for synthesis. The cell builds a second copy of every chromosome so each daughter cell can get a full set.

check.q: What is the job of a checkpoint in the cell cycle?
choices: To speed the cycle up
To pull the chromosomes apart
To pause the cycle until the cell confirms it is ready, such as checking that DNA is undamaged
To make the cell larger
check.why: Checkpoints are quality control. A cell that fails a check waits, repairs, or self-destructs.

check.q: Why does a serious injury to the brain heal so much worse than a cut on the skin?
choices: Brain cells have no DNA
The brain has no blood supply
Skin cells do not need to divide to heal
Mature nerve cells have mostly left the cell cycle and do not divide, while skin cells divide constantly
check.why: Healing depends on new cells. Skin is built to replace itself; most nerve cells are not.

lessons.title: Mitosis, Step by Step
lessons.mainIdea: Mitosis sorts two identical sets of chromosomes into two nuclei, and cytokinesis then splits the cell in two.
reading: In the 1880s the German anatomist Walther Flemming stained salamander cells with dyes and saw threads inside the nucleus thicken, line up, and pull apart in the dividing cell. He named the process *mitosis*, from the Greek for thread. The threads were chromosomes, though he did not know they carried genes. Under the microscope today, with a stain and a 400x objective, a root tip of an onion shows every stage he drew.

Before mitosis begins, S phase has already copied each chromosome. The two copies, called sister chromatids, stay attached at one point. In the first stage, prophase, the loose DNA coils tightly into short, visible chromosomes, the membrane around the nucleus breaks down, and a scaffold of protein fibers, the *spindle*, forms between the two ends of the cell. In metaphase, spindle fibers attach to each chromosome and line all of them up along the middle of the cell, like players at a center line.

In anaphase the sister chromatids are pulled apart, one copy toward each end of the cell. This is the moment that matters: each end now has a complete, identical set. In telophase the chromosomes uncoil, and a new nuclear membrane forms around each set. Finally, *cytokinesis* divides the cytoplasm. An animal cell pinches in at the middle until it splits. A plant cell, with its stiff wall, instead builds a new wall down the center. The result is two cells, each with the same 46 chromosomes as the original, for a human.

Mitosis is copying, not mixing. The daughter cells are genetically identical to the parent, which is exactly what you want when replacing skin, healing a cut or growing from a fertilized egg to an adult. This is Virchow's rule in action. A different kind of division, meiosis, makes sperm and egg cells with half the chromosomes each; it shuffles genes, and it belongs to the study of heredity.

words.d: the division of a cell's nucleus into two nuclei with identical sets of chromosomes
the framework of protein fibers that moves chromosomes during mitosis
the splitting of the cytoplasm into two cells after the nucleus divides
the two identical copies of a chromosome, joined together until anaphase

look.title: All Cells from Cells
look.text: Virchow insisted that where a cell arises, a cell must have existed before it, just as an animal comes only from an animal and a plant only from a plant. He rejected the older belief that cells could crystallize out of a formless fluid, and summed up his position in three Latin words: omnis cellula e cellula, every cell from a cell.
look.cite: Rudolf Virchow, lectures on cellular pathology, Berlin, 1855 to 1858
look.prompt: If every cell comes from a cell, then every cell in your body traces back through an unbroken chain of divisions. How far back does that chain go?

check.q: What happens during anaphase?
choices: Sister chromatids are pulled apart toward opposite ends of the cell
The DNA is copied
The nuclear membrane re-forms
The cell pinches into two
check.why: Anaphase is the separation step. Each end of the cell receives one complete set of chromosomes.

check.q: How do the two cells produced by mitosis compare to the original cell?
choices: Each has half the chromosomes
Each has the same chromosomes as the original
Each has twice the chromosomes
They have different, shuffled sets of chromosomes
check.why: Mitosis distributes two identical copies. Meiosis, a different process, halves and shuffles them.

check.q: Why does a plant cell finish dividing differently from an animal cell?
choices: Plant cells do not have a spindle
Plant cells copy DNA after mitosis
A plant cell has a rigid wall and cannot pinch in, so it builds a new wall down the middle
Plant cells have no cytoplasm
check.why: Cytokinesis in animals is a pinch. In plants it is a new wall laid across the center of the cell.

lessons.title: When Division Goes Wrong
lessons.mainIdea: Cancer is the result of damage to the genes that control the cell cycle, so cells divide without limit and spread.
reading: Every day, some of your cells suffer damage to their DNA, from sunlight, from chemicals, from ordinary copying mistakes. Nearly all of it is repaired or the damaged cell destroys itself at a checkpoint. But a few genes are the control system itself: genes that step on the gas of the cell cycle and genes that hit the brakes. If a cell collects mutations that jam the gas and cut the brakes, it divides when it should not, and its daughters do too. That is *cancer*. It is not one disease but hundreds, and each one begins as a cell breaking the rules of the cycle.

A clump of runaway cells is a *tumor*. If the cells stay in one place and keep their neighbors' boundaries, the tumor is *benign* and can usually be removed. A *malignant* tumor is one whose cells invade nearby tissue and, worst of all, travel through the blood or lymph to start new tumors elsewhere, a process called *metastasis*. Cancer cells also ignore the signals that tell normal cells to stop, evade the immune system, and grow new blood vessels to feed themselves. They are the body's own cells, following broken instructions.

What damages the control genes? Tobacco smoke is the largest preventable cause; its chemicals mutate DNA in the lungs, mouth and bladder. Ultraviolet light from the sun damages skin cell DNA. Some viruses insert their genes into ours; the human papillomavirus causes most cervical cancer, which is why there is now a vaccine against it. Some people inherit a faulty brake gene and start with one strike already. And time itself matters: the older a cell line, the more mutations it has had a chance to collect, which is why most cancers appear later in life.

Because cancer is division gone wrong, most treatments attack dividing cells. Radiation and many chemotherapy drugs damage DNA or break the spindle, which hits fast-dividing cancer cells hardest but also hits hair follicles and the gut lining, causing the familiar side effects. Newer drugs target the specific broken proteins in a patient's tumor. Much of what we know came from a single line of cells, taken in 1951 from a Baltimore woman named Henrietta Lacks, which has divided in labs around the world ever since. Her story also forced hard questions about consent that medicine is still answering.

words.d: a disease in which cells with damaged control genes divide without limit and may spread
a mass of cells produced by uncontrolled division
describing a tumor whose cells invade nearby tissue and can spread
the spread of cancer cells from the original tumor to other parts of the body
a change in the DNA sequence

look.title: What Cancer Is
look.text: The National Cancer Institute describes cancer as a disease in which some of the body's own cells grow out of control and spread to other parts of the body. It notes that cancer can begin almost anywhere in the trillions of cells of the human body, and that normally cells grow and divide to form new cells as the body needs them, dying when they are old or damaged and being replaced.
look.cite: U.S. National Cancer Institute, public information page on cancer, National Institutes of Health
look.prompt: The definition says cancer starts in the body's own cells. Why does that make it harder for the immune system to fight than an infection by bacteria?

check.q: What is the basic cause of cancer at the level of the cell?
choices: An infection by bacteria
A shortage of ATP
Cells losing their membranes
Mutations in the genes that control the cell cycle, so cells divide without limit
check.why: Cancer begins when the gas and brake genes of division are damaged. The cell keeps cycling when it should stop.

check.q: What makes a malignant tumor more dangerous than a benign one?
choices: Its cells invade nearby tissue and can spread to distant parts of the body
It grows faster in cold weather
It is always larger
It contains no DNA
check.why: Metastasis, the spread to new sites, is what makes cancer hard to remove and treat.

check.q: Why do many chemotherapy drugs cause hair loss?
choices: They are applied to the scalp
They attack rapidly dividing cells, and hair follicle cells divide rapidly too
Hair is made of cancer cells
They stop photosynthesis in the skin
check.why: Drugs aimed at dividing cells cannot tell a tumor cell from a fast-dividing normal cell in a hair follicle or the gut lining.

lessons.title: Stem Cells and Specialization
lessons.mainIdea: All your cells carry the same DNA; they differ because they read different genes, and stem cells are the ones that have not yet chosen.
reading: You began as one cell. Nine months later you were tens of trillions, of roughly 200 different kinds. The first cell divided by mitosis into two identical cells, then four, then eight. Somewhere along the way, cells that were identical began to differ. Some became muscle, some nerve, some blood, some bone. This narrowing of a cell's options is called *differentiation*. Once a cell has become a heart muscle cell, it and its descendants stay heart muscle.

Differentiation does not change the DNA. A nerve cell and a skin cell in the same person carry the same instructions. What differs is which genes are switched on. Signals from neighboring cells, from position in the embryo and from chemical gradients tell each cell which chapters of the DNA to read. A cell reading the muscle chapters fills with contracting proteins. A cell reading the blood chapters fills with hemoglobin and, in the case of a red blood cell, eventually throws away its nucleus.

A *stem cell* is a cell that has not finished choosing. It can divide to make more stem cells or produce cells that go on to specialize. The cells of a very early embryo are *pluripotent*: they can become any cell type of the body. Adult stem cells are more limited. The ones in your bone marrow can make any kind of blood cell, but not nerve or muscle. That is what a bone marrow transplant is: giving a patient whose blood-making stem cells were destroyed by disease or by cancer treatment a new supply from a donor.

In 2006, the Japanese scientist Shinya Yamanaka showed that adding just four genes could turn an ordinary adult skin cell back into a pluripotent stem cell. He shared a Nobel Prize for it in 2012. These induced pluripotent stem cells let researchers grow a patient's own nerve or heart cells in a dish to study a disease or test a drug. Growing whole replacement organs remains far harder than headlines suggest, but the basic finding stands: specialization is a setting, not a permanent rewrite, and it can be reset.

words.d: the process by which a cell becomes a specialized type by switching certain genes on and off
a cell that can keep dividing and can produce specialized cells
able to become any of the body's cell types
a stretch of DNA that carries the instructions for one protein or one trait

look.title: The Same Book, Different Chapters
look.text: Picture a library where every reader is handed the same thick book. One reader is told to read only the chapters on cooking, another only the chapters on carpentry, a third only on music. By the end of the year, each is an expert in something different, though the books on their desks are identical.
look.prompt: In this picture, what stands for the DNA, and what stands for the signals that tell a cell what to become? Where would a stem cell fit?

check.q: A muscle cell and a nerve cell from the same person have different shapes and jobs. What is the reason?
choices: They have different DNA
Muscle cells have more chromosomes
They switch on different genes and so build different proteins
Nerve cells have lost most of their genes
check.why: Differentiation is about gene use, not gene content. The instructions are the same; the reading differs.

check.q: What can a bone marrow stem cell do that a mature red blood cell cannot?
choices: Carry oxygen
Live in the blood
Fit through capillaries
Keep dividing and produce new blood cells of different kinds
check.why: Stem cells retain the ability to divide and to produce specialized descendants. A mature red blood cell has no nucleus and cannot divide.

check.q: Why was Yamanaka's 2006 discovery important?
choices: It showed that a specialized adult cell can be reset to a pluripotent state, so specialization is not permanent
It proved that all cells have different DNA
It made mitosis unnecessary
It showed stem cells only exist in embryos
check.why: Four added genes turned skin cells back into stem cells, a result that changed both the science and the ethics of stem cell research.

lessons.title: Systems Working Together
lessons.mainIdea: Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form systems, and no system does its job alone.
reading: Take a single stride during a run and count what has to happen. Muscle cells in your leg burn ATP. To recharge it they need oxygen and glucose, delivered by blood. The blood is pushed by the heart and loaded with oxygen in the lungs. Breathing speeds up because sensors in the brain notice rising carbon dioxide. The glucose came from a meal, broken down in the gut and stored in the liver. Sweat glands dump heat. Kidneys adjust water and salt. One stride, and most of your body is involved.

Biologists describe this as levels of organization. Cells of the same type working together form a *tissue*, such as muscle tissue or nerve tissue. Several tissues combined into a structure with a job form an *organ*: the heart is muscle tissue, nerve tissue, connective tissue and a lining, all working together. Organs that cooperate on a larger task form an *organ system*. The heart, blood vessels and blood make up the circulatory system. The human body has about a dozen such systems.

The key idea is that systems interact. The circulatory system carries what the respiratory system takes in and what the digestive system absorbs. The nervous system and the hormones of the endocrine system coordinate the rest, using the feedback loops from the last chapter. The skeletal and muscular systems move the whole thing around. The excretory system, mainly the kidneys, cleans the blood that every other system has been dumping waste into. Damage one system and the others feel it: a failing heart leaves the kidneys short of blood, and failing kidneys let waste build up that poisons the heart.

Step back and the whole unit fits together. Water and carbon build molecules. Molecules build cells. Cells run on ATP made from sugar that came, through a plant, from sunlight. Cells divide by mitosis, specialize, and organize into tissues, organs and systems that keep the inner environment steady. Priestley's mint and Priestley's mouse were the two halves of one loop. You are the mouse's side of it, made of about 37 trillion cells, every one of them descended from a single cell by the process in this chapter.

words.d: a group of similar cells working together on one job
a structure made of several tissues that performs a specific function, such as the heart
a group of organs that work together on a larger task, such as circulation
the heart, blood vessels and blood, which carry materials throughout the body

look.title: One Missed Meal
look.text: A student skips breakfast and lunch, then plays a full soccer match after school. Late in the second half she feels shaky and dizzy and cannot think clearly. A teammate hands her a juice box, and within ten minutes she feels almost normal.
look.prompt: Trace what happened through at least three organ systems, from the empty stomach to the shaky legs and back. Which feedback loop from the last chapter was involved?

check.q: Which sequence correctly lists levels of organization from smallest to largest?
choices: Organ, tissue, cell, organ system
Cell, tissue, organ, organ system
Tissue, cell, organ system, organ
Organ system, organ, tissue, cell
check.why: Cells make tissues, tissues make organs, and organs make organ systems.

check.q: During a run, your breathing speeds up. Which two systems are most directly coordinating this?
choices: The skeletal and digestive systems
The excretory and skeletal systems
The nervous system sensing carbon dioxide and the respiratory system responding
The digestive and endocrine systems
check.why: Sensors in the brain detect rising carbon dioxide and signal the breathing muscles to work harder.

check.q: A patient's kidneys fail. Why do doctors worry about the heart as well?
choices: The kidneys pump blood to the heart
The heart is made of kidney tissue
Kidney failure stops the heart from beating instantly
Wastes the kidneys normally remove build up in the blood and harm the heart, because organ systems depend on each other
check.why: No system works alone. The blood the heart pumps is the blood the kidneys are supposed to clean.

review.q: What did Priestley's mint do to the air in the sealed jar, in modern terms?
choices: It took in carbon dioxide and released oxygen by photosynthesis
It absorbed the smoke from the candle
It cooled the air so the candle could burn
It released carbon dioxide for the mouse to breathe
review.why: The candle had used up oxygen; the plant restored it while consuming the carbon dioxide the candle had produced.

review.q: Which correctly states the overall inputs and outputs of photosynthesis?
choices: Glucose and oxygen in; carbon dioxide and water out
Carbon dioxide and water in; glucose and oxygen out
Oxygen and water in; glucose and carbon dioxide out
Glucose and water in; oxygen and carbon dioxide out
review.why: Plants take in carbon dioxide and water, use light energy, and produce glucose and oxygen.

review.q: Which stage of cellular respiration produces the most ATP, and where does it happen?
choices: Glycolysis, in the cytoplasm
Fermentation, in the cytoplasm
The electron transport chain, in the inner membrane of the mitochondrion
The Calvin cycle, in the stroma
review.why: The electron chain and the ATP-making enzyme in the inner mitochondrial membrane produce most of the roughly 30 ATP per glucose.

review.q: A cell has plenty of glucose but no oxygen. What can it do?
choices: Run full aerobic respiration anyway
Switch to photosynthesis
Stop making ATP entirely
Use fermentation to keep glycolysis going, yielding only 2 ATP per glucose
review.why: Fermentation frees the electron carriers so glycolysis can continue without oxygen, at a much lower yield.

review.q: The Mauna Loa carbon dioxide record rises and falls each year. What causes the yearly dip?
choices: Northern Hemisphere plants photosynthesizing during their growing season
Volcanic eruptions on Mauna Loa
Ice melting in the Arctic
Animals breathing less in summer
review.why: When the vast land areas of the Northern Hemisphere leaf out, net photosynthesis draws carbon dioxide down for several months.

review.q: Put these in the correct order for a dividing cell.
choices: Mitosis, then DNA copying, then growth
Growth, then DNA copying, then mitosis, then cytokinesis
Cytokinesis, then mitosis, then DNA copying
DNA copying, then cytokinesis, then mitosis
review.why: G1 growth comes first, S phase copies the DNA, mitosis separates the sets, and cytokinesis splits the cell.

review.q: What is a checkpoint, and why does its failure matter for cancer?
choices: A place where cells exchange nutrients; failure causes starvation
A membrane channel; failure lets water in
A pause in the cell cycle where damage is detected; failure lets damaged cells keep dividing
The point where chromosomes line up; failure stops mitosis
review.why: Checkpoints catch damaged DNA. When the genes running them are mutated, damaged cells escape and can become tumors.

review.q: A skin cell and a nerve cell in one person differ because:
choices: They inherited DNA from different parents
Nerve cells have lost the skin genes
Skin cells have extra chromosomes
They express different sets of the same genes
review.why: Differentiation switches genes on and off. Every body cell keeps the full set of instructions.
